subject: technology

essential_question: How can understanding patterns, sequences, and introductory algorithms help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
learning_objectives: Build a clear mental model of everyday sequences through an explicit worked example, demonstration, text, or phenomenon.
Use subject-appropriate evidence or representation to communicate understanding of everyday sequences.
Check, revise, or improve work about everyday sequences using stated success criteria.
lesson_success_criteria: The learner completes the central task about everyday sequences.
The learner gives evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer.

materials: unit-specific source, model, manipulatives, safe materials, or approved digital tool
task_brief: This is day 2 of "Patterns, Sequences, and Introductory Algorithms". That is unit 4 in grade 3. Today is a worked-model trace about everyday sequences. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Write and test a step-by-step set of directions for a partner or character to follow. Today helps by working on everyday sequences. Your unit also covers what is an algorithm, everyday sequences, giving step-by-step directions, and following a partner's directions. Today is for practice. You are scored on finishing and being honest, not on getting it perfect.
primary_task: Use the whole example printed in activity_setup about everyday sequences. Follow it one step at a time. Do not skip ahead. After each step, write what changed. Make a small table. Show what things looked like before and after each step. Now change one thing in the example. Guess what will happen. Then check. Was your guess right? Last, say the rule for everyday sequences in your own words. Everything you need is printed in activity_setup. It has the exact case, what should happen, how to try it, checks, and a paper choice worth the same score. Do not wait for another handout or app. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about everyday sequences. It is part of "Patterns, Sequences, and Introductory Algorithms". Later days in this unit cover other things, like what is an algorithm. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about everyday sequences; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 3 you need one clear try with a grown-up nearby. Say or write your reason in a sentence or two. Drawings, objects, or spoken answers are all fine.

central_input.title: Inline everyday sequences code case
central_input.purpose: Use this exact fictional case to investigate everyday sequences; no other file, model, dataset, or account is needed.

expected_behavior_and_specification: The procedure must execute every supplied step in order; the main input must return open > check > save.
An empty step list must return an empty string, and a one-step list must retain that step.
The submitted explanation must connect the observed control flow or data state to everyday sequences, not merely state the final number.
The smallest test case must be tried and its actual result compared with the expected result.

execution_method.primary: No-install browser method: open any browser developer console, paste the complete starter code, press Enter, and record the output or exact error text.
execution_method.local_optional: If Node.js is already installed, save the unchanged snippet as activity.js and run `node activity.js`; installing Node.js is not required.
execution_method.no_computer_required: The hand-trace route below is a complete execution method and earns identical credit.

debugging_target.observed_failure: Iteration begins at index 1, so the first instruction is silently skipped and the main input returns check > save.
debugging_target.target: Repair the initial index, explain the sequence invariant, and rerun all three tests.
debugging_target.passing_change: Iteration begins at index 0; all three tests retain every step in order.
debugging_target.scope_note: Diagnosing the state, control-flow, or data defect and connecting the repair to everyday sequences is the central evidence.

equal_credit_alternative.method: Paper or notes-app simulation; this earns exactly the same score as running code.
steps: Make one row for each statement or loop check and copy the starting input exactly.
Record every variable, object field, selected item, and output after that step.
Circle the first row where the actual state stops matching the specification.
Apply the one repair named in your explanation and trace all three tests again.
equal_credit_alternative.evidence_to_submit: The completed trace, the one-line corrected condition, and an expected-versus-actual table for all three tests.

test_or_check_criteria: Your table has one row for each step and shows things before and after.
Each step has a short reason why it is right.
You changed one thing, guessed what would happen, and then checked.
You said the rule for everyday sequences in your own words.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: You can do this with the keyboard only, no mouse needed. Text can be made bigger, and you may do it on paper instead of a screen.
Anything you have to study will also come as plain text, a described version, or a version you can touch.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never require a real password, private message, precise location, account credential, API key, or identifiable image.
Use only fictional or sandboxed systems, accounts, and data; never probe, exploit, or attempt to access a real external system.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify, not as an authority or a substitute for learner work.
The tutor may explain, demonstrate, or debug alongside the learner, but must not silently complete a graded project or assessment for them.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting everyday sequences.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for everyday sequences follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for everyday sequences, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for everyday sequences works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of everyday sequences, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking everyday sequences mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply everyday sequences under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on everyday sequences rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
